4. The other distinction between the Old and New Testaments is established in figures: because the former, in the absence of the truth, showed only an image and a shadow instead of the body, whereas the latter exhibits the present truth and the solid body. And mention is made of this almost everywhere the New Testament is opposed to the Old; yet its treatment in the Epistle to the Hebrews is more extensive than anywhere else. There, the Apostle argues against those who thought that the observances of the Mosaic Law could not be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the whole of religion. To refute this error, he assumes <margin>Psalm 110:4</margin> what had been predicted by the Prophet concerning the priesthood of Christ. For since an eternal priesthood is conferred upon Him, it is certain that that priesthood is abolished where successors were substituted for one another daily. He proves, moreover, that the institution of this new priest prevails because <margin>Heb. 7:11, 19; 9:9; 10:1</margin> it is established by an oath. He adds afterward that in that transfer of the priesthood, a change of the Testament is also involved. And he confirms that this was necessary by reasoning that such was the weakness of the Law that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to what that weakness was: namely, that it had external justifications of the flesh which could not render its worshippers perfect in conscience, and that through the sacrifices of beasts, it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it was a shadow of future good things in itself, not the living image of the things; and therefore, it had no other office than to be an introduction into a better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. Here it must be observed in what respect the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, and the ministry of Christ with the Mosaic. For if the comparison were to pertain to the substance of the promises, a great discord would exist between the two Testaments; but since the state of the question leads us elsewhere, we must aim to discover the truth. Let us, therefore, place in the middle the covenant which is eternal and will never perish. Christ is the completion of it, from whom it finally has its status and validity. While such confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are as it were the solemn symbols of confirmation. This was the point of contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. These, even though they were only accidents of the covenant, or at least accessories and annexes, and (as the common parlance goes) accessories; yet because they were instruments for administering it, they have the name of a covenant, just as is accustomed to be given to other <term>Sacraments</term> <gloss>sacred signs</gloss>. Therefore, in summary, the Old Testament is called in this place the solemn method of confirming the covenant, comprehended in ceremonies and sacrifices. And so, because there is nothing solid underlying it unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be antiquated and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the sponsor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification was once acquired for the elect, and transgressions which remained under the Law were obliterated. But if you prefer it simply, understand it thus: the Old Testament of the Lord was that which was delivered wrapped in the shadowy and ineffective observation of ceremonies. And therefore it was temporary, because it was, as it were, in suspense until it was supported by a firm and substantial confirmation. Then, at last, it became new and eternal after it was consecrated and established by the blood of Christ. Whence Christ calls the cup which He proffers to the disciples in the Supper the cup of the New Testament <margin>Matt. 26:28</margin> in His blood: to signify that then truly does God's Testament possess its own truth, through which it becomes new and eternal while it is sealed by His blood.

5. From this it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that the Jews were led by the pedagogy of the Law <margin>Galat. 3:24; 4:1</margin> to Christ before He Himself was exhibited in the flesh. He acknowledges that they also were children and heirs of God, but who, because of their childhood, had to be held under the custody of a pedagogue. For it was fitting, as the sun of righteousness had not yet risen, that there should be neither such a brilliance of revelation nor such a perspicacity of understanding. Thus, therefore, the Lord dispensed the light of His Word to them, so that they might see it from afar and still obscurely. Therefore, Paul marks this thinness of intelligence with the word childhood, by which the Lord willed them to be exercised in the elements of this world and in small external observances, as if they were rules of childish discipline, until Christ should shine forth: through whom the knowledge of the faithful people had to grow. Christ Himself marked this distinction when He said that the Law and the <margin>Matt. 11:13</margin> Prophets were until John, and from that time the kingdom of God is evangelized. What did the Law and the Prophets profit the men of their own time? Namely, they provided a taste of that wisdom which was one day to be manifested clearly, and they prefigured it as it shone from afar. But when Christ can be pointed out with the finger, the kingdom of God has been opened. For in Him are exposed all the treasures of <margin>Coloss. 2:9</margin> wisdom and intelligence, by which one penetrates almost to the very inner sanctuaries of heaven.

<summary>This page explores the distinction between the Old and New Testaments, explaining that the Mosaic Law served as a pedagogical shadow and temporary confirmation of the eternal covenant, which reached its completion and solidity only through the person and blood of Christ.</summary>
